title: Gateway pathing & fallback playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic playbook for gateway pathing and graceful fallback across regions. Focus is on predictable behavior when traffic crosses region boundaries, how/where mTLS should be terminated/passthrough, and tradeoffs for running a lightweight gateway-only footprint vs full sidecar mesh in each region.

Context / problem statement:
- We run low-latency inference workloads across multiple regions. Traffic patterns are bursty and occasionally imbalance when customers flood a single region.
- Goals: preserve SLOs (p50/p95), minimize cross-region egress cost, avoid cascading failures when a regional control plane is unhealthy, and keep the security posture (mTLS + cert rotation) auditable.

Design principles:
- Region-first routing: prefer regional model replicas and regional gateways for latency/cost, with controlled cross-region fallback when capacity exhausted.
- Explicit control-plane/data-plane separation: make control-plane decisions (policies, rollouts) eventually consistent; keep data-plane routing decisions fast and local where possible.
- Least privilege trust domains: gateways terminate mTLS only when they are the policy boundary; otherwise use passthrough to downstream services with short-lived downstream certs.
- Observable failover: every fallback must create an event and metric (fallback_count, fallback_reason, latency_spike).

High-level topology options (tradeoffs):
1) Gateway-only regional mesh (recommended for lightweight infra)
   - Each region runs a pair of edge gateways (active/standby) and a small fleet of L7 gateways that handle TLS, auth, rate-limit, routing into regional pools.
   - No ubiquitous sidecar; services expose an internal port and are reached by regional gateways through internal L4 paths.
   - Pros: lower overhead, easier ops, simpler certificate model.
   - Cons: coarser routing granularity, harder to do per-service canaries without additional tooling.

2) Full sidecar mesh per region (fine-grained control)
   - Sidecars provide per-pod routing, mTLS enforcement, telemetry. Connect gateways to sidecar-injection networks.
   - Pros: rich policy, per-service canary, better circuit breaking, localized failover.
   - Cons: CPU/memory overhead; more complex cert distribution; higher operational surface area.

3) Hybrid: gateway-only for public ingress, sidecars for critical internal services
   - Use gateway-only for high-scale stateless inference workers; sidecars for stateful control services (metadata, rollout orchestrators).

Control plane split patterns:
- Central coordinator / Regional pilots: global control plane distributes policy bundles; small regional pilot translations apply to local proxies.
- Soft-control: policy updates are published with TTLs; in absence of coordinator, region falls back to last-known-good bundle.
- Heartbeat and quorum: regional pilots report health to central coordinator; central only forces global rollback if >N regions unhealthy.

Routing policy examples:
- Latency-first: prefer same-region replicas; route to cross-region only if local queue_time > threshold or capacity_utilization > 85%.
- Cost-first: prefer regional spot pools or quantized cheaper instances; only route to high-cost pools when latency budget allows.
- Priority-tiered routing: premium customers pinned to dedicated capacity; public pool used only when premium pool saturated (with immediate fallback event).

mTLS trust model patterns:
1) Terminate at edge gateway (TLS offload)
   - Use for public ingress where edge needs to apply WAF, auth introspection, header enrichment.
   - Gateway holds a TLS cert from KMS/HSM; internal traffic re-encrypted with short-lived regional certs.
2) Passthrough to internal gateway/sidecar
   - Edge performs SNI-based routing and passes TLS. Downstream sidecar terminates; allows end-to-end client identity.
   - Useful when client identity must be preserved to service.
3) Hybrid: TLS offload + downstream mTLS for service-to-service
   - Offload for inspection, then establish mTLS for internal trust.

Certificate lifecycle and rotation:
- Root CA: stored in HSM, rotated infrequently (every 2–3 years).
- Regional intermediate CAs: rotate every 3 months; automated via CA-service and signed by root.
- Short-lived service certs: 1–7 day TTL issued by regional pilot.
- Rollout strategy: phased rotation – pilot region, canary, global. Make sure old certs remain valid for a grace window to avoid mass connection drops.

Cross-region fallback & failover sequence (intentional order):
1) Local gateway rejects new session if acceptance policies exceed threshold (rate/queue). Return 429 with fallback_hint header.
2) Client SDK honors fallback_hint to attempt adjacent-region gateway (backoff + jitter).
3) Gateway in adjacent region applies cost/latency checks; if acceptable, route; otherwise start tiered queuing.
4) If global capacity exhausted, degrade to reduced-quality model variant (e.g., smaller context length, quantized model) and emit fallback event.

Observability and runbooks:
- Mandatory metrics: regional_ingress_rps, regional_success_rate, fallback_count, cross_region_egress_bytes, cert_rotation_failures, connection_drain_time.
- Distributed tracing: ensure trace IDs survive gateway handoffs. Add trace-sampled headers when doing passthrough/termination.
- Logs: structured JSON with fields region, gateway_id, fallback_reason, model_variant, customer_tier.
- Quick triage commands: curl with SNI to region gateway, tcpdump on gateway NIC, check pilot bundle age (pilotctl bundle-age), and list active certs (certctl list --region).

Resilience knobs and tuning:
- Circuit breaker thresholds: per-service p95 latency and error rate thresholds that trip to fallback; use gradual ramp-back.
- Connection draining: on gateway subnet scale-down, mark node draining, stop accepting new sessions, wait for in-flight tokens (max drain_timeout), then terminate.
- SYN backlog tuning: increase SYN backlog and tune TIME_WAIT reuse for heavy burst traffic.
- Autoscaling: scale by queue length and per-GPU utilization, prefer warm-up short bursts vs cold start capacity.

Security considerations:
- KMS/HSM integration for CA private keys; audit logs for every issuance.
- Limit admin/control-plane access to bastion with short-lived SSH certs.
- Rate-limit control-plane API calls to prevent policy churn floods.

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs:
- How aggressive should cross-region fallback be vs preferring degraded model variants? (latency vs correctness tradeoff)
- Certificate grace windows: how large to tolerate to avoid partial disconnects during rotation?
- Sidecar cost threshold: define exact CPU/RAM delta where we flip from gateway-only to sidecar. Need bench numbers per model size.
- Observability overhead: how much tracing sampling is ok for production without exploding storage cost?

Action items / next steps:
- (A) Run a small experiment: deploy gateway-only in eu-west and us-west with passthrough enabled for internal control services. Measure cross_region_egress_bytes & p95 impact. Owner: Maya. Due: 2024-03-15.
- (B) Create a cert-rotation playbook with explicit rollback steps, add certctl commands and test in staging. Owner: Ethan. Due: 2024-03-08.
- (C) Define SLOs for fallback_count and implement a fallback alert (pager when fallback rate > 0.5% for >5min). Owner: Alex. Due: 2024-03-10.

Notes / references:
- See CON-4523 for historical incidents where cross-region fallbacks increased egress costs.
- Benchmark risk: quantized models saved 25% CPU but increased p95 by ~30ms in our internal tests (JIRA-PLAT-1210).

Appendix: sample gateway config snippets (pseudo)
- Latency-first routing rule:
  match: request.region == client.region && pool.utilization < 0.85
  action: route to pool.local
  else: route to pool.adjacent region with fallback_header

- Fallback header example:
  X-RI-Fallback: region=us-west-2; reason=capacity; policy=degraded_model

End of playbook.

(Informal notes style: rough edges are intentional; hand this to SRE + platform eng for iteration.)
